title: ‘Living in Water’ is an exercise in empathy
summary: 'We don't experience the climate crisis the same way,' says journalist Ana P. Santos

blocks.text: 'We don't experience the climate crisis the same way,' says journalist Ana P. Santos

items: The documentary 'Living in Water' provides an immersive 360 virtual reality experience of life in Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan, highlighting the regular flooding faced by residents due to climate change.
Investigative journalist Ana P. Santos aims to bridge the empathy gap for viewers unfamiliar with the struggles of those living in flood-prone areas, showcasing personal stories of island residents.

Despite the challenges of frequent flooding, many residents, like Riri Sacdalan, express a deep attachment to their home, emphasizing their unwillingness to leave the island where they have lived their entire lives.

MANILA, Philippines – What is it like to live with floodwater? The people in Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan tell their story in the 360 virtual reality documentary ‘Living in Water.’

Flooding is a regular occurrence in a country beset by an average of 20 storms a year, but some places experience harsher conditions. Investigative journalist Ana P. Santos wanted the format to create an empathy exercise for viewers who do not have quite the same relationship with water as the people in Isla Tibaguin.

“Hindi lahat tayo pare-pareho ng nararanasan ng climate crisis,” Santos said on Saturday, November 21, during a talkback in Rappler’s Social Good Summit 2026. (We don’t experience the climate crisis the same way.)
The documentary takes the viewer, who wears a headset wrapped around their head, in an immersive 360 experience of the flooded island.

Viewers can look around and inspect their surroundings, adopting the perspective of a person standing in the middle of the flooded area. The only thing missing is the wet sensation of water around the legs.

“‘Yung experience ko o ‘yung gusto sana nating ipahiwatig sa paggawa ng isang virtual reality and 360 immersive experience ay ‘yung pag bridge ng understanding, at ‘yung pag bridge ng empathy gap,” Santos said.
(My experience, or what we wanted to convey using the virtual reality and 360 immersive experience, is to bridge understanding and the empathy gap.)

The film was shown in sessions with limited audience during Rappler’s summit. Furnitures inside houses are partly submerged, a mother cooks a meal for their family standing on floodwaters, and children wade outside to play.
The documentary followed island residents Riri Sacdalan and Angie Atieza. They joined Santos in the talkback. Atieza shared that she was happy they got to share their story.

“Kasi tanong nga po namin, paano kaya nila mararamdaman ‘yung nararamdaman namin?” Atieza said on Saturday. “Kung sila ang nasa sitwasyon namin, kaya kaya nila tulad namin?” (That was our question, how will they feel what we feel? If they were in our position, will they endure like us?)

The film showed Atieza cooking for her children, talking with the barangay chairperson, and visiting the flooded village hall. The documentary also showed Sacdalan waking up to floodwaters, his grandmother sitting idly on a bed immersed in water.
Rising seas are driven by climate change and a warming world. In the Philippines, this is exacerbated by flood control infrastructure that turned out to be ghost projects or substandard ones.

Between living with regular floods and leaving the place they call home, many residents chose to stay. An immediate solution that residents can resort to, if they have the money to do so, is to raise their houses from the ground.
“Para sa akin sa totoo lang, hindi ko po magawang umalis sa isla,” Sacdalan shared with the audience. (For me, in truth, I can never leave the island.)
“Kaya ko nasabi po na dito ako pinanganak, dito ako lalaki, dito ako tatanda, dito ako mamamatay. Kasi po nandodoon po ang buhay namin.”
(I have said that this was where I was born, this is where I will grow up, grow old, and die. This is where our life is.) – Rappler.com
